candidateRows: Philosophy's search for strict definitions and essential properties is ill suited to free will and should yield to population thinking.
This methodological claim explains why the dispute persists and supports Dennett's broader effort to replace metaphysical essences with practically grounded capacities.
After the host asks why free will remains disputed after millennia, Dennett diagnoses a foundational methodological error in philosophy and recommends a Darwinian alternative.
Free will remains disputed because it bears directly on responsibility and spans metaphysical, ethical, political, existential, and conceptual questions.
The move establishes why definitions of free will, desert, and responsibility matter and frames the practical and conceptual terrain of Caruso's case.
Dennett's claim that philosophy's definition-centered method explains the debate's persistence.
Caruso supplements the methodological diagnosis by arguing that the issue persists because it crosses several philosophical domains and cannot be settled by science alone.
Libertarian free will has no coherent model, and randomness cannot supply the relevant agency because the real issue is control rather than causation.
The argument removes libertarian alternatives while identifying control as the capacity that matters, thereby clearing the ground for Dennett's compatibilist account.
The preceding discussion of libertarian theories and whether philosophical progress has improved them.
Following discussion of libertarian positions, Dennett argues that neither a nonphysical inner agent nor quantum chance produces freedom, while ordinary unpredictability can serve autonomous control.
Introducing indeterminacy into deliberation does not create desert-grounding freedom because the agent still cannot settle which supported outcome occurs.
This supplies Caruso's control-based objection to naturalistic libertarianism and explains why reason-supported random outcomes cannot ground the responsibility at issue.
Dennett's dismissal of libertarian models and his claim that randomness does not provide control.
Caruso grants that sophisticated libertarian accounts improve on crude randomness but argues that replaying an indeterminate choice would expose an uncontrolled distribution of outcomes.
Because persons and actions ultimately result from factors beyond their control, basic-desert responsibility is absent whether the universe is deterministic or indeterministic.
This is Caruso's core thesis connecting ultimate lack of control to denial of basic-desert responsibility independently of the truth of determinism.
The host's pragmatic proposal that society might assume determinism even if individuals experience free choice.
In answering a pragmatic question, Caruso first defines his skepticism and separates it from a simple commitment to determinism, locating the dispute in basic desert.
Practices that intentionally harm people on desert grounds require strong warrant for the requisite freedom, and unresolved disagreement leaves that burden unmet.
The move converts skepticism about free will into a direct normative challenge to retribution while preserving the possibility of non-desert consequentialist measures.
The host's suggestion that practical social benefits might justify adopting a useful assumption about free will.
Caruso argues that intentionally harmful responsibility practices are not innocuous and that proponents must justify the freedom and desert those practices presuppose.
The freedom worth wanting is practical self-control, and responsibility-supporting laws and sanctions are necessary to sustain a secure cooperative society.
This directly answers Caruso by grounding responsibility in observable capacities rather than metaphysical independence and by defending the social necessity of punishment.
Caruso's epistemic argument that uncertainty about desert makes intentionally harmful responsibility practices unjustified.
Dennett argues that responsibility tracks whether agents can control themselves, that capable agents must maintain that control, and that legal sanctions help secure social cooperation.
Determinism does not eliminate the relevant ability to do otherwise because people can respond to persuasion, change their conduct, and develop moral competence.
The argument directly supplies the reasons-responsive compatibilist capacity at the heart of the motion and rejects determinism as a barrier to genuine practical alternatives.
The skeptical implication that determinism prevents agents from doing otherwise in a responsibility-grounding sense.
After the host asks whether controlled agents could have acted otherwise, Dennett identifies practical changeability and competence as the relevant basis for responsibility.
Free-will skepticism denies only basic-desert responsibility for backward-looking praise, blame, punishment, and reward, not every form of responsibility.
The distinction blocks the claim that skepticism abolishes all responsibility and sharply defines the exact desert-based target of Caruso's challenge.
Dennett's contention that free-will skepticism encourages people to deny that anyone is ever responsible.
Caruso begins his response to Dennett by distinguishing basic-desert responsibility from other responsibility notions that skepticism can leave intact.
Free-will skepticism rejects basic-desert responsibility while preserving causal and attributive responsibility and forward-looking moral engagement.
The distinction identifies exactly which form of responsibility skepticism denies and which responsibility practices remain available without desert.
Dennett's suggestion that free-will skepticism discards responsibility as a whole.
After Dennett dismisses metaphysical free will, Caruso narrows his skepticism to basic desert and preserves responsibility grounded in moral formation, reconciliation, and safety.
The core dispute is whether a desert system should be preserved when free will is defined as the control required for basic-desert responsibility.
This move fixes the debate's central conception of free will and directly challenges whether backward-looking desert should survive at all.
Dennett's consequentialist justification for retaining desert-based responsibility practices.
Caruso marks broad agreement on forward-looking practices, then locates disagreement in desert, defines the relevant freedom, and questions preserving desert within Dennett's system.
Basic moral desert is a misleading construct, while sufficient ordinary moral responsibility can justify coercion, imprisonment, fines, and reputational consequences.
Dennett rejects Caruso's framing and asserts that practical responsibility sufficient for legal and social sanctions does not require ultimate desert.
Caruso's claim that preserving a system of basic desert requires separate justification.
Dennett calls basic desert a red herring and uses an unreformed offender to argue that the state may impose serious consequences on a sufficiently responsible agent.
Coercion and liberty restriction can be justified by self-defense, public safety, and least-restrictive means without invoking free will, retribution, or basic desert.
The quarantine model supplies the skeptic's central alternative foundation for state coercion and rebuts the claim that desert is needed for public protection.
Dennett's contention that rejecting basic desert leaves inadequate grounds for coercing serious offenders.
Caruso accepts state coercion but grounds it in protection rather than punishment, applying the quarantine analogy to officeholding restrictions and less-punitive criminal responses.
Deterministically produced differences in reasons, character, and action do not justify differential praise, blame, punishment, or reward on basic-desert grounds.
The paired deterministic-universe case directly argues that agents are not the ultimate sources needed for desert even when their actions and characters differ.
Caruso contrasts a robber and charitable donor in deterministic universes, removes forward-looking benefits, and argues that neither is an appropriate source for basic desert.
Deterministic causation does not eliminate control because autonomous agents become largely self-made through sustained learning, reflection, practice, and moral education.
This is the principal compatibilist reply to source incompatibilism: responsibility rests on developed self-control rather than impossible absolute self-creation.
Caruso's argument that deterministic histories prevent Maya and Marina from being responsible sources.
Dennett says the thought experiment omits upbringing and self-control, then grounds responsibility in agents' long development and allows punishment of an autonomous wrongdoer.
An undamaged, informed, reasons-responsive, self-controlled person can meaningfully be said to have been able to do otherwise despite determinism.
The move supplies a naturalistic compatibilist interpretation of alternative possibilities and connects responsibility to ordinary capacities rather than metaphysical branching.
The challenge that the example assumes the offender genuinely could have acted otherwise.
After abnormal brain conditions are distinguished, Dennett explains ordinary ability to do otherwise through freedom from restraint, damage, deception, and impaired rational control.
Reasons-responsiveness and other compatibilist distinctions matter for rehabilitation and proportionate sanctions but do not by themselves ground desert-based blame or punishment.
This concession isolates the precise inferential dispute: skeptics accept differences in agency while denying that those differences establish basic-desert responsibility.
Dennett's use of reasons-responsiveness and self-control to distinguish responsible from impaired agents.
Following examples of severely impaired offenders, Caruso accepts the distinction between responsive and unresponsive agency but assigns it forward-looking rather than desert-based significance.
Compatibilist agent control and freedom from intentional external manipulation are distinct, and possessing agent control leaves open whether basic-desert responsibility is justified.
The argument targets a central compatibilist premise by denying that internal reasons-responsive control alone settles responsibility under manipulation, luck, or determinism.
Dennett's distinction between causation and control as a sufficient answer to skeptical challenges.
Caruso separates internal agent control from an external manipulator's control, accuses Dennett of privileging the latter threat, and invokes several incompatibilist arguments against sufficiency.

A malfunctioning brain implant can generate conduct while leaving compatibilist psychological conditions intact, challenging accounts that require an intentional external manipulator to undermine responsibility.
The case tests whether compatibilist control conditions are sufficient by presenting nonintentional causal determination that appears responsibility-undermining despite reasons responsiveness.
Dennett's response that manipulation cases threaten responsibility because external agents intentionally control the person.
Caruso describes Elizabeth's therapeutic implant malfunction, an induced egoistic desire, and her continued satisfaction of compatibilist conditions despite no intentional manipulating agent.
Causal determination by ordinary history is not relevantly different from determination by a malfunctioning implant merely because no external manipulator is involved.
The proposition directly contests the compatibilist attempt to distinguish responsibility-undermining manipulation from ordinary deterministic causation.
Dennett's claim that responsibility is removed specifically when another agent or company exercises control.
After Dennett attributes the implant malfunction to the manufacturer, Caruso argues that the agent's determining psychological states are equally caused under natural determinism.
Control exercised by other agents matters because social institutions must address deliberate interpersonal interference, unlike causation by impersonal natural history.
This supplies the compatibilist's principal distinction between manipulation cases and ordinary causal determination of an agent's psychology.
Caruso's argument that distinguishing external control from natural causation assumes the very issue in dispute.
Dennett answers the implant challenge by grounding the distinction in social and political facts about agents who intentionally interfere with others' activities and control.
A forward-looking public-health model can preserve legal distinctions among intentional, accidental, and habitually negligent conduct by tracking future danger and appropriate protection.
The argument answers the practical objection that rejecting basic desert would erase legally important distinctions among offenses and offenders.
The challenge that existing degrees of homicide and punishment may not be maintainable within Caruso's proposed system.
Caruso compares deliberate killing, an isolated tragic lapse, and habitual negligence, tying different protective responses to intent, character, causal involvement, and prospective risk.
A purely future-risk model implies that a deliberate murderer should be released immediately after taking a reliable treatment that eliminates all future danger.
The hypothetical exposes a demanding consequence of grounding incapacitation solely in prospective dangerousness rather than culpability or desert.
Caruso's claim that protective intervention should vary according to the offender's future threat rather than basic desert.
Dennett tests the quarantine model with a deliberate killer who ceases to be dangerous through a hypothetical treatment and therefore appears to qualify for release.
If a treatment genuinely removes an offender's future threat, incapacitation is no longer justified, though real interventions would raise independent ethical and autonomy concerns.
The reply accepts rather than evades the strongest implication of the forward-looking model while separating incapacitation grounds from treatment ethics.
Dennett's treatment hypothetical alleging that a future-risk model must release a previously deliberate murderer.
Caruso accepts release under the stipulated facts, while arguing that actual transformative technologies would require reconsideration of consent, autonomy, rehabilitation, and forms of confinement.
Determinism and free-will skepticism do not reduce persons to inert tools because rational deliberation, persuasion, belief change, and reasons-responsive action remain causally effective.
This directly defends the human capacity for reasons-responsive control while denying that such control establishes the disputed kind of free will.
The objection that skepticism treats humans as deterministic machines whose behavior is merely adjusted like a tool.
Caruso agrees that arguments can change minds and actions, but maintains that this ordinary efficacy of reasons is fully consistent with both determinism and denial of free will.
Public, proportionate punishment sustains respect for law and supports a consequentialist notion of desert that does not depend on whether determinism is true.
The argument connects reasons-responsiveness to responsibility practices and explains why compatibilist desert remains socially valuable without metaphysical indeterminism.
Caruso's contention that rational deliberation survives determinism while free will and desert-based punishment can still be rejected.

Dennett argues that functioning legal institutions require known rules and proportionate sanctions, with responsible agents recognizing their liability while impaired agents receive different treatment.
Replacing punishment with medical treatment risks indefinite confinement, while adequate safeguards would make the quarantine model functionally equivalent to humane nonretributive punishment.
This challenges the practical distinctness and protective adequacy of the skeptical alternative to punishment, a major responsibility-practices issue.
Caruso's proposed quarantine framework and his objection that Dennett inaccurately characterizes it as medicalized punishment.
Dennett warns that treatment language can conceal lifelong institutionalization and argues that a properly constrained quarantine regime ultimately becomes a system of humane punishment.
Consequentialist punishment can preserve transparency, deterrence, and contractualist protections without free will, leaving desert rather than punishment as the genuine dispute.
The argument directly denies that valuable responsibility practices establish compatibilist free will and isolates the contested role and strength of desert.
Dennett's claim that maintaining respected laws, public sanctions, and humane punishment supports compatibilist free will and desert.
Caruso argues that skeptics may accept many institutional goods Dennett invokes, then presses whether Dennett's residual desert is thin enough to be shared or robust enough to need defense.
Basic moral desert names a nonexistent requirement, whereas familiar everyday desert is grounded in conduct and reasons and remains independent of determinism.
This defines the pro side's operative conception of desert and rejects the skeptical definition that makes stronger metaphysical authorship a condition of free will.
Caruso's demand that Dennett specify whether his preserved desert is merely thin or a robust and philosophically controversial notion.
Dennett dismisses basic moral desert while defending an ordinary comparative and conduct-sensitive conception of deserving that he regards as compatible with deterministic causation.
Determinism does not defeat moral responsibility, because socially embodied responsibility practices legitimately include ordinary desert, blame, punishment, and agents taking responsibility.
This directly defends the motion’s central claim that natural moral competence sustains responsibility and desert independently of determinism or indeterminism.
Caruso's claim that Dennett preserves only a weak practice while retaining dangerously loaded desert terminology.
Dennett answers the proposed terminological retreat by identifying the responsibility practices he seeks to preserve and grounding them in agents’ moral competence.
Because responsibility practices are socially evolved and historically changeable, society can further reform them by relinquishing harmful notions of just desert and retribution.
The argument challenges the inference from the evolutionary naturalness of responsibility practices to their continued justification in their present desert-based form.
Dennett's appeal to the evolved emotional and social foundations of blame, punishment, and responsibility practices.
Caruso accepts the evolutionary account of responsibility practices but uses their historical malleability to support further reform away from desert and retribution.
A free-will skeptic can justify punishment, deterrence, separation, and self-protection on forward-looking grounds without invoking basic moral responsibility or retributive desert.
This contests the alleged practical necessity of compatibilist desert by arguing that the example’s defensible responses remain available under free-will skepticism.
The preceding infidelity thought experiment offered to show that guilt, punishment, and deserved blame require robust responsibility.
Caruso separates permissible protective and deterrent responses from retributive reactions, maintaining that the former do not distinguish Dennett’s position from skepticism.
The evolutionary naturalness of reactive attitudes does not give them justificatory authority, especially for retributive law and public policy.
The move blocks a naturalistic justification of retribution and argues that ordinary desert language can provide conceptual cover for punitive practices both speakers oppose.
The appeal to evolved moral emotions as necessary, authentic mechanisms for communicating blame and sustaining punishment.
Caruso distinguishes the origin of reactive attitudes from their normative authority, disputes their use to justify retributive law, and urges abandoning loaded desert language.
Society should retain moral responsibility and punishment while rejecting basic moral desert and retributive punishment, since consequentially justified punishment is not retribution.
Dennett draws the central boundary of his position: responsibility and punishment remain valuable practices even though basic desert and retribution should be discarded.
Caruso's proposal that both sides should unite against retributivism by abandoning desert terminology that gives it cover.
Dennett accepts historical moral reform but denies that reform requires eliminating punishment or responsibility, distinguishing them from basic desert and retribution.
If backward-looking desert performs genuine justificatory work in Dennett's punishment theory, the theory is mixed rather than purely consequentialist; if it performs none, desert should be removed.
This dilemma targets whether desert adds any indispensable justification to Dennett’s responsibility practices and therefore probes the substantive difference between the two positions.
Dennett's claim that his account preserves punishment and responsibility through consequentialist justification without becoming retributive.
Caruso argues that consequentialism can justify the same practices without desert, forcing Dennett either to identify desert’s additional work or concede its dispensability.
A consequentialist justification can establish a rule-governed punishment system while individual adjudication properly ignores case-specific outcome calculations and enforces agreed rules.
The move explains how a forward-looking justification of the institution can coexist with backward-looking, rule-based judgments in individual cases without ad hoc consequentialism.
Caruso's claim that purely consequentialist punishment can preserve the relevant practices without any independent role for desert.
Dennett uses sports officiating to distinguish justification of an entire practice from its internal application, defending stable rules and penalties against individualized calculation.
Equal and transparent rule enforcement can itself be justified by its consequences, so causal responsibility can identify whom to sanction without adding desert as an independent ground.
This reply attempts to absorb Dennett’s rule-enforcement model into a desert-free consequentialism and renews the dilemma over whether his account is genuinely mixed.
Dennett's referee analogy and claim that agreed rules must govern particular punishments without case-specific consequentialist calculation.
Caruso grants that uniform rule enforcement improves the account but argues that its benefits and backward-looking causal assignment do not require moral desert.

Game penalties do not establish philosophically significant moral desert, because social punishment and reactive attitudes have higher stakes, greater harms, and distinct condemnatory and communicative functions.
The distinction challenges Dennett’s principal analogy by denying that instrumental rule enforcement in games vindicates desert in morally consequential social practices.
Dennett's use of deserved sports penalties to model punishment, blame, and responsibility within society's rule-governed practices.
Caruso accepts limited similarities between games and society but argues that game blame lacks the philosophically important features at issue in the free-will debate.
Serious game penalties properly carry moral condemnation and desert, and society likewise depends on members accepting blame and punishment for violating its constitutive rules.
This directly links rule-governed desert to the maintenance of a free and secure society and asserts that its legitimacy is independent of luck and determinism.
Caruso's claim that game blame lacks the condemnatory, communicative, and high-stakes features of interpersonal responsibility.
Dennett argues that egregious sports violations already bear moral significance, then generalizes the model to social membership, blame, punishment, and civic security.
Enforcing social and interpersonal rules can be justified while resentment, indignation, and moral anger remain separately open to challenge.
The distinction separates justified behavioral regulation from the desert-laden reactive attitudes challenged by the skeptical side.
Dennett's defense of enforceable rules and responsibility practices as necessary safeguards against social corruption.
After discussion of cheating and institutional enforcement, Caruso accepts the need for rules but redirects the dispute toward whether punitive reactive attitudes are justified.
Because evolved responsibility practices are revisable, desert-dependent anger can be replaced by attitudes such as disappointment or sorrow without losing practical benefits.
The proposal directly supports the con side's case that effective responsibility practices do not require basic desert or its associated moral anger.
Dennett's contention that culturally evolved responsibility practices and emotional responses perform indispensable regulatory work.
Caruso argues that philosophical reflection can modify inherited practices while preserving most social responses and replacing a limited set of desert-presupposing attitudes.
The naturalness and inevitability of resentment do not establish its justification, and reflective agents can deny such emotions justificatory authority.
This argument blocks an inference from evolved human emotional capacities to the normative legitimacy of desert-based blame and punishment.
The compatibilist appeal to natural human reactions and culturally evolved practices as components of justified responsibility.
Caruso distinguishes experiencing an involuntary emotional response from endorsing it as a reason for further treatment, sanctions, or interpersonal action.
Disappointment may guide children, but serious wrongdoing by competent adults can justify moral anger that also warns others against similar misconduct.
The response defends both the fittingness and the forward-looking signaling function of moral anger against the proposed skeptical replacement.
Caruso's proposal to replace resentment and moral anger with disappointment, sorrow, and other non-desert attitudes.
Dennett grants that disappointment can be more effective with a young child but argues that adult wrongdoing warrants stronger condemnation with broader deterrent value.
